category: X11-F2 Detection of fabricated objects by depth, context or physical plausibility
title: Protecting Autonomous Cars from Phantom Attacks
key_idea: Journal article on protecting cars from phantom attacks; its one-sentence record abstract says it enables object detectors to better separate real from fake objects in semi-autonomous and fully autonomous vehicles.
method: Not read in this run. The CCS 2020 paper by the same first author (row P2-P402 of LIT_A4) describes a committee of four small CNNs (light, context, surface, depth) that judges each detected object; whether this article presents the same countermeasure is UNVERIFIED.
relation_to_project: Detection side of the phantom lead and the closest prior work to any camera-only real-versus-fake object check on slides 01, 03 and 04: the owner cues must be compared with it at matched false-alarm points. Full text needed before citing.
notes: Crossref record matches (journal-article, 2023); the record abstract is one sentence. A DOI recalled from memory for this article resolved to an unrelated paper; the DOI here comes from a Crossref title search. Article type and review status in the magazine not checked. NEEDS_VERIFY: relation to the CCS 2020 paper (journal-length version or new material), evaluation data and false-alarm numbers.

title: MobilBye: Attacking ADAS with Camera Spoofing
key_idea: A drone-carried portable projector presents a spoofed traffic sign to a driving car and the Mobileye driver-assistance unit reads it as a real sign; colour, shape, projection speed, diameter and ambient light are varied.
method: Physical experiment: spoofed signs injected into a Mobileye unit by projection while sign colour, shape, projection speed, diameter and ambient light are changed.
data: Mobileye external driver-assistance unit; drone with a portable projector; a driving car (abstract).
reported_result: Abstract: the unit can be made to interpret the drone-carried spoofed sign as a real traffic sign; no rates given.
relation_to_project: Earliest record found here for the part of the owner abstract about objects that are not there: a commercial unit accepts a sign that does not exist. The varied factors (projection speed, diameter, ambient light) are the factors a light or plausibility cue would be tested on.
notes: Preprint, not peer reviewed. Precursor of the CCS 2020 phantom paper (row P2-P402 of LIT_A4). Projector medium, so it belongs with the LIT_A4 family; kept here because no other task had catalogued it when this row was written.

title: bAdvertisement: Attacking Advanced Driver-Assistance Systems Using Print Advertisements
venue: 2022 IEEE European Symposium on Security and Privacy Workshops (EuroS&PW)
key_idea: Title-level: an attack on advanced driver-assistance systems delivered through print advertisements, a creation medium that needs no projector or screen (abstract not read).
method: Not read.
data: Not read.
relation_to_project: Non-projector member of the phantom family: printed matter carries no projected-light signature, so the slide 04 light cues would not apply and appearance, context and geometry cues (slide 01) must carry the check. Needs a full-text read.
notes: Crossref record has no abstract. From memory, UNVERIFIED: a road sign embedded in a print advertisement is picked up by a production driver-assistance system. NEEDS_VERIFY: target systems, sign types, success rates and any countermeasure.

title: Seeing isn't Believing
venue: Proceedings of the 2019 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security
key_idea: Robust physical adversarial examples for detectors in two forms: a hiding attack and an appearing attack whose nested design joins two patterns so a false object is detected at long and short distance.
method: Hiding: feature-interference reinforcement and enhanced realistic constraints generation. Appearing: nested adversarial example that combines two examples, made in varied styles to look less suspicious.
data: YOLO V3 and Faster R-CNN; distances 1 m to 25 m and angles -60 to 60 degrees; three further black-box models (arXiv abstract).
reported_result: arXiv abstract: success rate up to 92.4% over 1 m to 25 m and -60 to 60 degrees; high transfer to three black-box detectors.
relation_to_project: Defines the printed appearing attack for the claim about obstacles that are not there: a flat pattern reported as an object across a range of distances. Test material for a slide 01 shape or geometry check and for slide 05, because the nested design aims at a false object that stays detected from far to near (per-frame persistence is not given in the abstract).
notes: The Crossref title field holds only the main title. The arXiv preprint (2018) is titled Seeing isn't Believing: Practical Adversarial Attack Against Object Detectors; the abstract was read from the arXiv record, so numbers may differ from the CCS text. Which object classes the appearing attack fabricates is not in the abstract.

title: Fooling the Eyes of Autonomous Vehicles: Robust Physical Adversarial Examples Against Traffic Sign Recognition Systems
venue: Proceedings 2022 Network and Distributed System Security Symposium
key_idea: Pipeline for physical adversarial examples against detector-based traffic sign recognition on streaming video, covering four attack vectors: hiding, appearance, non-target and target attacks.
method: Image-transformation distribution extended with blur and resolution changes to imitate in-vehicle cameras; single and multiple bounding-box filters for efficient perturbation training.
data: YOLO v5 based traffic sign recognition; sunny, cloudy and night illumination; a 2021 model production vehicle (abstract).
reported_result: Abstract: examples are effective and robust against the YOLO v5 system and transfer to other detectors; hiding and non-target attacks succeeded on the 2021 vehicle. No rates in the part of the abstract read.
relation_to_project: Sign-specific creation attack (the appearance vector) with night-time tests, matching the project night focus. The abstract reports vehicle tests only for the hiding and non-target attacks, so real-vehicle evidence for a fabricated sign is not shown in the text read.
notes: Crossref (NDSS 2022) and arXiv records both checked. Abstract read to its first 1,800 characters (cut where a discussion of three items begins). Appearance Attack is taken to mean a sign reported where none exists, the usual meaning; the definition is not in the part read: UNVERIFIED.

title: Rogue Signs: Deceiving Traffic Sign Recognition with Malicious Ads and Logos
key_idea: Sign Embedding attack: innocuous signs and advertisements are modified so that a traffic sign recogniser classifies them as an attacker-chosen traffic sign with high confidence, so no existing sign needs to be touched.
method: Adversarial optimisation over a set of image transformations; printed samples tested in drive-by runs at varied distance, lighting and camera angle, plus virtual tests.
data: Printed adversarial signs and logos; drive-by tests; virtual evaluation (abstract).
reported_result: Abstract: adversarial success rates above 95% in both physical and virtual settings.
relation_to_project: Print-medium creation attack on sign recognition: a non-sign object is read as a traffic sign. Direct case for slide 01: a shape and placement check asks whether the carrier has legal sign geometry. Classifier-level; the abstract does not attack the detection stage.
notes: Preprint, not peer reviewed as read; a workshop publication may exist (not checked). Companion preprint DARTS is row P2-P2007.

title: DARTS: Deceiving Autonomous Cars with Toxic Signs
key_idea: Two ways to make toxic signs: out-of-distribution attacks that start from arbitrary images instead of real signs, and a lenticular printing attack that uses an optical effect to fool sign recognition.
method: Out-of-distribution adversarial examples and lenticular printing; virtual and real-world tests under white-box and black-box threat models.
data: Traffic sign recognition models; virtual and real-world settings (abstract).
reported_result: Abstract: attacks succeed in both settings and both threat models; out-of-distribution attacks can outperform in-distribution attacks on adversarially trained classifiers. No rates in the abstract.
relation_to_project: Adds two creation media beyond stickers: arbitrary non-sign images and lenticular prints. From memory, UNVERIFIED: a lenticular print shows different content at different viewing angles, which would make it a direct test for the viewpoint-conditioned check of slide 01.
notes: Preprint, not peer reviewed as read. The viewing-angle property of lenticular printing is not stated in the abstract (it says an optical phenomenon): check the full text. Overlaps with row P2-P2006 by the same first author.

title: Poltergeist: Acoustic Adversarial Machine Learning against Cameras and Computer Vision
venue: 2021 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP)
key_idea: Title-level: acoustic signals are used as an adversarial channel against cameras and computer vision (abstract not read). A later paper describes camera signal injection as adding image distortion (see notes).
method: Not read.
data: Not read.
relation_to_project: Creation medium with no visible object, sticker or light source in the scene. From memory, UNVERIFIED: sound aimed at the camera stabiliser blurs frames so that detectors hide, create or alter objects. If so, the cue to test is frame blur and motion consistency (slide 05), not object appearance.
notes: Crossref record has no abstract. TPatch (row P2-P2009) builds on acoustic signal injection toward cameras and names hiding, creating and altering attacks in its abstract. NEEDS_VERIFY: mechanism, targets and success rates of this paper.

title: TPatch: A Triggered Physical Adversarial Patch
key_idea: A printed patch stays benign until acoustic signal injection toward the camera adds a designed distortion; it then launches a hiding, creating or altering attack on detectors and classifiers, with content-based camouflage.
method: Patch optimised to act only under the injected distortion; content-based camouflage against driver suspicion; robustness enhancement for the physical world.
data: YOLO V3, YOLO V5 and Faster R-CNN detectors and eight image classifiers; simulation and real-world tests (abstract).
reported_result: Abstract: effective in simulation and in the real world on the three detectors and eight classifiers; no rates given. Defences at the sensor, algorithm and system levels are discussed.
relation_to_project: A patch-induced creating attack that is switched on only at chosen moments: a patch scan on untriggered frames sees a harmless picture. The trigger is an image distortion, so a frame-quality or blur cue (slide 05) might mark the moment of attack (hypothesis, not tested).
notes: Preprint record (record year 2023); a security-conference publication is recalled from memory, venue UNVERIFIED. Builds on the acoustic channel of row P2-P2008.

title: DoubleStar: Long-Range Attack Towards Depth Estimation based Obstacle Avoidance in Autonomous Systems
key_idea: Light from two complementary sources exploits stereo matching and lens flare to inject fake obstacle depth into stereo cameras, so an obstacle-avoidance system reacts to an obstacle that is not there.
method: Two attack formats, projected light beams and lens-flare orbs; tests on two commercial stereo cameras, an Ardupilot simulation and a commercial drone.
data: ZED and Intel RealSense stereo cameras; Ardupilot simulation; one commercial drone with obstacle avoidance (abstract).
reported_result: Abstract: fake depth created up to 15 m away at night and up to 8 m in daytime; a flying drone is repeatedly brought to a sudden stop or drifted away, even bypassing sensor fusion mechanisms.
relation_to_project: Warning for depth-based plausibility checks: a stereo depth cue can itself be made to report a fake obstacle, so depth is not an attack-free referee. Gives a false-stop outcome measured on a real drone; road-vehicle tests are not in the part of the abstract read.
notes: Preprint record; a security-conference publication is recalled from memory, venue UNVERIFIED. Light-based medium, so it also belongs with the LIT_A4 family (not catalogued there when this row was written). Abstract cut at 1,800 characters before the mitigation part.

title: TOG: Targeted Adversarial Objectness Gradient Attacks on Real-time Object Detection Systems
key_idea: Three perturbation attacks on real-time detectors named by their effect: object-vanishing, object-fabrication and object-mislabeling, plus a universal variant that transfers to black-box models at negligible attack-time cost.
method: Targeted objectness-gradient attacks on the detection network (the name of the method); a universal objectness-gradient variant uses adversarial transferability for black-box attacks on edge systems.
data: PASCAL VOC and MS COCO; YOLO and SSD (abstract).
reported_result: Abstract: serious vulnerabilities shown on both detectors and both data sets; no numbers given.
relation_to_project: Supplies the effect taxonomy (vanish, fabricate, mislabel) used in the problem map and a simple generator of fabricated boxes for controlled tests. Image-space perturbation with no physical object, so it is a digital stand-in only.
notes: Preprint, not peer reviewed as read. A 2020 conference paper by the same first author with a near-identical title (Adversarial Objectness Gradient Attacks in Real-time Object Detection Systems, IEEE TPS-ISA, DOI 10.1109/tps-isa50397.2020.00042) is in the Crossref ledger; that it is the published version of this preprint is UNVERIFIED.

title: Physically Realizable Adversarial Creating Attack Against Vision-Based BEV Space 3D Object Detection
key_idea: Title-level: a physically realizable creating attack against vision-based bird-eye-view 3D object detection, the camera-only 3D detection setting of driving stacks (abstract not read).
method: Not read.
data: Not read.
relation_to_project: Most recent journal record found here for a camera-only creation attack in 3D detection space, where a fabricated object would get a position on the road and could enter planning. Medium, carrier and success rates are unknown. Needs a full-text read through the library route.
notes: Crossref record has no abstract. NEEDS_VERIFY: attack medium (patch, poster or object), detectors, data sets and any defence discussion.

title: Daedalus: Breaking Nonmaximum Suppression in Object Detection via Adversarial Examples
key_idea: Adversarial examples shrink detection boxes so that non-maximum suppression no longer merges them, leaving extremely dense false positives; an ensemble of substitute models gives black-box transfer, and printed posters carry the attack.
method: Optimisation that compresses box dimensions to evade non-maximum suppression; ensemble of popular detection models as substitutes; poster demonstration.
data: End-to-end detection models (names not in the abstract); printed posters against real-world detection systems.
reported_result: arXiv abstract: false positive rate raised to 99.9% and mean average precision reduced to 0 at low distortion; the attack is also shown with printed posters.
relation_to_project: Fabrication at scale: a flood of false boxes instead of one phantom. A cheap count-and-density sanity check on detector output would probably flag it (hypothesis), which makes it an easy positive class and a contrast to single-object phantoms.
notes: Crossref (journal, 2022) and arXiv (2019) records both checked; the journal title writes Nonmaximum as one word. Numbers come from the arXiv abstract and may differ in the journal text.

title: Phantom Sponges: Exploiting Non-Maximum Suppression to Attack Deep Object Detectors
venue: 2023 IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV)
key_idea: A universal perturbation adds many phantom objects that overload non-maximum suppression and slow each frame, while the original objects stay detected so that the attack is noticed later.
method: Universal adversarial perturbation aimed at the non-maximum suppression stage of the detection pipeline while preserving the original detections.
data: Not named in the abstract.
reported_result: Abstract: processing time of individual frames increases; no numbers given.
relation_to_project: Availability attack through fabricated detections: it targets the latency budget that Paper 2 promises to keep. A lightweight monitor must not itself scale with the number of boxes, and any ms-per-frame claim should state behaviour under a box flood.
notes: Crossref (WACV 2023) and arXiv (2022) records both checked; abstract read from the arXiv record. Image-space universal perturbation, not a printed patch; the projector-based physical counterpart is SlowPerception (row P2-P525 of LIT_A5).

title: TrackFlood: Relocating Latency Attacks from NMS-Free Detectors to Real-Time Trackers
key_idea: For detectors without non-maximum suppression, perturbations flood the multi-object tracker with spatially spread phantom detections; a bounded-admission layer that caps tracker workload restores latency at a cost in admitted clean detections.
method: White-box overload attack on detect-then-track pipelines with one-to-one and query-based detectors; a lightweight, architecture-agnostic admission cap is evaluated as the defence.
data: YOLOv10, YOLO26 and RT-DETR with trackers on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, TensorRT FP16 (abstract).
reported_result: Abstract: detector latency stays essentially constant while tracker latency rises; at the standard budget (L-infinity 8/255) the end-to-end slowdown is modest with no deadline misses for association-dominated trackers; a higher-budget stress test gives severe slowdowns and sustained deadline misses.
relation_to_project: Recent embedded-hardware evidence that fabricated detections cost compute downstream, plus a simple rejection rule (cap admissions) with a stated price in lost true detections: the trade-off any plausibility filter for phantom objects has to report.
notes: Preprint, not peer reviewed. Image-space white-box perturbation, not a physical attack. Abstract cut at 1,800 characters.

title: Exploring the Vulnerability of Single Shot Module in Object Detectors via Imperceptible Background Patches
key_idea: Small perturbations placed only in background patches, outside every object box, cut true positives and sharply raise false positives, because the effective receptive field of single-shot modules is larger than the object.
method: Search for a few background patches and imperceptible perturbations on them, against region proposal networks and single-stage detectors.
data: MS COCO 2014; 5 two-stage and 8 single-stage detectors (abstract).
reported_result: Abstract: true positives decrease and false positives increase dramatically across the 13 detectors; no numbers given.
relation_to_project: False detections caused from outside the object region: a check that inspects only the detected box (the slide 01 ROI) would not see the cause. Imperceptible image-space patches, so this is evidence about detector mechanics, not a physical threat.
notes: Preprint, not peer reviewed as read; published venue not checked.

title: APRICOT: A Dataset of Physical Adversarial Attacks on Object Detection
key_idea: Title-level: a dataset of physical adversarial attacks on object detection (abstract not read). From memory, UNVERIFIED: photographs of printed patches built to make detectors report a chosen object class.
method: Not read.
data: APRICOT (title). Size, patch types and licence not read.
relation_to_project: Candidate real-photo test set for patch-induced false detections: a positive class for a fabricated-object check without printing patches. Row P2-P110 of LIT_A1 reports a pixel-level re-annotation named APRICOT-Mask. Licence and download terms must be recorded before any use.
notes: Crossref type book-chapter, 2020; the conference name is not shown in the record (recalled as ECCV 2020, UNVERIFIED). NEEDS_VERIFY: whether the patches are targeted (object-creating), image count, scenes and licence.

title: Detecting Adversarial Perturbations in Multi-Task Perception
venue: 2022 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
key_idea: Flags adversarial inputs when edges extracted from the image, the predicted depth and the predicted segmentation disagree; an edge-consistency training loss tightens the benign agreement first.
method: Multi-task network (depth estimation and semantic segmentation); edge inconsistency score across the three modalities; a multi-task attack aimed at both tasks and at the detection scheme is also built.
data: Cityscapes and KITTI (abstract).
reported_result: Abstract: under an assumed 5% false positive rate up to 100% of images are correctly detected as perturbed, depending on perturbation strength.
relation_to_project: CLOSEST PRIOR WORK found here to a camera-only depth and structure consistency check: independent cues, a disagreement score and a fixed false-positive operating point. It handles image-level digital perturbations, not physical fabricated objects; no per-object decision and no abstain state in the abstract.
code_or_data: https://github.com/ifnspaml/AdvAttackDet (named in the abstract; not opened) UNVERIFIED
notes: Crossref (IROS 2022) and arXiv records both checked; abstract read from the arXiv record. Code licence not checked. Whether the edge-consistency score reacts to a depthless phantom (a projected or printed object) is untested in the text read.

category: X11-F2 Detection of fabricated objects by depth, context or physical plausibility
title: Connecting the Dots: Detecting Adversarial Perturbations Using Context Inconsistency
key_idea: Learns context consistency rules during training and checks them at test time: one auto-encoder per object class outputs a discrepancy when a perturbation makes an object out of place in its scene.
method: Detector augmented with class-specific auto-encoders over context information; the input-output discrepancy signals a violated context rule.
data: PASCAL VOC and MS COCO (abstract).
reported_result: Abstract: ROC-AUC over 0.95 in most cases, more than 20% better than a context-agnostic method.
relation_to_project: Context check that can reject an object that does not fit its scene, the natural test for a fabricated sign or obstacle. General-scene data, not driving. Row P2-P516 of LIT_A5 (ADC) reports attacks built to evade context checks, so an adaptive test is required.
notes: Crossref book-chapter record (2020; conference name not shown, recalled as ECCV 2020, UNVERIFIED) and arXiv record both checked; abstract read from the arXiv record. Which attack goals (misclassify, hide, appear) were tested is not stated in the abstract. The language-model variant by Yin et al. is row P2-P126 of LIT_A1 and is not repeated here.

category: X11-F2 Detection of fabricated objects by depth, context or physical plausibility
title: Shadow-Catcher: Looking into Shadows to Detect Ghost Objects in Autonomous Vehicle 3D Sensing
key_idea: Validates each object reported by a LiDAR 3D detector through a physical invariant, its 3D shadow; ghost objects created by spoofed returns are flagged when the shadow is anomalous.
method: Shadow analysis per detected object in the point cloud; end-to-end prototype; tested against invalidation attacks that target the defence itself.
data: KITTI (abstract).
reported_result: arXiv abstract: more than 94% accuracy in identifying anomalous shadows for vehicles, pedestrians and cyclists; 0.003 s to 0.021 s on average per object on commodity hardware; 2.17x speedup over prior work.
relation_to_project: LiDAR analogue of slide 02: a shadow used as a physical invariant to reject fabricated objects, per object and in milliseconds. The cue is a point-cloud shadow, not a photometric one, so the idea transfers to a camera and the method does not.
notes: Also catalogued by LIT_A2 as row P2-P234 (metadata-only there); this row adds the abstract read from the arXiv record (2020). The Crossref book-chapter record (2021) does not name the conference. Sensor is LiDAR, outside the camera-only scope: kept as an analogue.

category: X11-F2 Detection of fabricated objects by depth, context or physical plausibility
title: Exorcising ''Wraith'': Protecting LiDAR-based Object Detector in Automated Driving System from Appearing Attacks
key_idea: Plug-in module beside a LiDAR detector removes forged obstacles whose local parts score low objectness; the predictor uses the physical relation between depth and point density, which appearing attacks violate.
method: Local objectness predictor with explicit depth input; obstacles with a major share of low-objectness parts are eliminated; closed-loop control driving tests in simulation with Baidu Apollo.
data: Three known appearing attacks on LiDAR detectors; simulation-based closed-loop tests on Apollo (abstract).
reported_result: Abstract: at least 70% of forged cars eliminated in most cases, against under 30% for the best earlier defence, with less overhead in car AP and precision than existing defences.
relation_to_project: Template for a per-object fabricated-object filter: part-level evidence plus a distance-dependent physical prior, scored by forged objects removed and by precision lost on real ones, then checked in closed loop. LiDAR only; a camera analogue (apparent size and detail against distance) is untested.
notes: Preprint record; a security-conference publication is recalled from memory, venue UNVERIFIED. Sensor is LiDAR, outside the camera-only scope: kept as an analogue and because it names the appearing-attack class. A related LiDAR record read but not catalogued: Sun et al. 2020 (arXiv 2006.16974, occlusion patterns as physical invariants).

category: X11-F2 Detection of fabricated objects by depth, context or physical plausibility
title: Formalizing and evaluating requirements of perception systems for automated vehicles using spatio-temporal perception logic
venue: The International Journal of Robotics Research
key_idea: Spatio-Temporal Perception Logic expresses requirements on perception output streams with spatial and temporal operators, allowing basic sanity checks of a perception system even without ground truth in some cases.
method: Logic over perception data across frames; a fragment is monitorable offline in polynomial time; example specifications for vehicle perception systems.
data: Not named in the abstract.
reported_result: Abstract: a polynomial-time offline-monitorable fragment is identified and a range of perception specifications is presented; no numbers.
relation_to_project: A formal, explainable language for plausibility rules on detector output, for example that an object should not appear from nowhere at close range (our example, not from the abstract). A violated formula is itself the explanation. Offline monitoring only in the abstract; not an attack paper.
notes: Crossref record with abstract. Related records found by title search and not catalogued (no abstract in Crossref): Dokhanchi et al. 2018, quality temporal logic, DOI 10.1007/978-3-030-03769-7_23; Balakrishnan et al. 2021, PerceMon online monitoring, DOI 10.1007/978-3-030-88494-9_18.

title: Too Afraid to Drive: Systematic Discovery of Semantic DoS Vulnerability in Autonomous Driving Planning under Physical-World Attacks
venue: Proceedings 2022 Network and Distributed System Security Symposium
key_idea: Treats overly conservative planning as a security problem: harmless-looking physical objects placed by an attacker, such as off-road cardboard boxes, cause failed or badly degraded missions; PlanFuzz finds such cases.
method: Dynamic testing with planning invariants as test oracles, constrained input generation for attacker-placed objects and a vulnerability distance metric that guides the search.
data: 3 planning implementations from practical open-source driving systems; simulation and real-vehicle traces for case studies (abstract).
reported_result: Abstract: 9 previously unknown semantic denial-of-service vulnerabilities found without false positives.
relation_to_project: Question 3 evidence, not a fabricated-object paper: it measures needless stopping at the planning layer through planning invariants. A false-braking measure for phantom objects could reuse such invariants as the oracle (hypothesis).
notes: Crossref (NDSS 2022) and arXiv records both checked; abstract read from the arXiv record. A 2022 workshop demo record with the same title exists in Crossref (not catalogued). Objects here are real and harmless, not fabricated; filed under F1 because that family carries the false-stop consequence. Abstract cut at 1,800 characters.

title: Does Physical Adversarial Example Really Matter to Autonomous Driving? Towards System-Level Effect of Adversarial Object Evasion Attack
venue: 2023 IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV)
key_idea: Measurement study: published STOP-sign evasion attacks are evaluated in a full driving pipeline and none produces a system-level effect such as a traffic rule violation; a system-driven attack design (SysAdv) raises the violation rate.
method: System-level evaluation with the full driving pipeline, a vehicle plant model and physically consistent object sizes; new attack design built on the two limitations found.
data: Representative prior STOP-sign evasion attacks; full driving-system context (abstract).
reported_result: Abstract: all representative prior works achieve no system-level effect; with SysAdv the violation rate rises by around 70%.
relation_to_project: Question 3 evidence: the published template for system-level measurement covers object evasion (a missed stop), not object creation. No matching measurement study for false braking caused by fabricated objects was found in this run, so that measure looks open, to our knowledge.
notes: Crossref (ICCV 2023) and arXiv records both checked; abstract read from the arXiv record. Evasion attack, outside the fabricated-object families: filed under F1 as the comparison point for consequence measurement. A 2024 demo record with the same title exists in Crossref (not catalogued).

title: Evaluating Adversarial Attacks on Driving Safety in Vision-Based Autonomous Vehicles
key_idea: End-to-end evaluation framework with driving-safety metrics for perturbation and patch attacks on stereo 3D object detectors; the attack impact on detection precision and the impact on driving safety turn out to be decoupled.
method: Evaluation of two vision-based 3D detectors under two attack types with a set of driving safety performance metrics; ablation study on the causes of the findings.
data: Stereo R-CNN and DSGN 3D object detectors (abstract).
reported_result: Abstract: impact on driving safety and impact on detector precision are decoupled; DSGN is more robust than Stereo R-CNN. No numbers in the abstract.
relation_to_project: Question 3 evidence: detector-level scores do not predict driving-level harm, so a false-alarm or false-braking claim for Paper 2 needs a driving-level measure. Which safety metrics are used, and whether needless braking is among them, is not in the abstract.
notes: Crossref (journal, 2022) and arXiv (2021) records both checked; abstract read from the arXiv record. Not a fabricated-object paper: filed under F1 for the consequence-measurement question. NEEDS_VERIFY: list of safety metrics in the full text.
